cards.lead: Solar horizon calendar at Chankillo in the Andes
cards.note: The sources date the towers to between 200 and 300 BCE (a Daily Star report of the 2007 Science paper), not c. 250-200 BCE, and the Yale release gives approximately the 4th century BCE, so the lead's narrower range is not kept. Nothing opened says the observatory was independent, so origin is unknown.
cards.name: Solar horizon observatory at Chankillo, Peru
cards.summary: Thirteen towers at Chankillo on the Peruvian coast were read as a solar observatory that marks sunrise and sunset through the year, the earliest complete one known in the Americas.
cards.description: Thirteen towers built north to south on a ridge inside the Chankillo complex line up with two viewing points, so that from them the towers span the sun's rising and setting arcs across the year. Ghezzi and Ruggles argued this in a 2007 Science paper, which press reports describe as a calendar accurate to within a few days. The Yale release calls it the earliest known complete solar observatory in the Americas that defines all the major aspects of the solar year.
cards.origin_note: The sources describe the observatory as the earliest of its kind in the Americas but do not state whether it was reached without knowledge of other solar observatories, so independence is not established.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead: a single site's calendar with no successor shown in the sources opened, and the Inka sun-pillar link is unestablished.

events.label: between 200 and 300 BCE

events.quote: the sequence of towers erected between 200 and 300 BC

open_questions: The Daily Star gives 200-300 BCE and the Yale release gives approximately the 4th century BCE; the 2007 Science paper itself was not opened, and a 2016 radiocarbon and tree-ring study (Ghezzi, Hogg et al.) reportedly gives a narrower range that was not fetched.
Whether any continuity with the Inka sun pillars near Cusco can be shown: the Yale release says those pillars have vanished and their location is unknown.
The coordinates are approximate, from general knowledge, and not from a fetched source.

cards.lead: Geometric planetary astronomy in the Greek world
cards.note: Sources date Hipparchus's dated observations on Rhodes to 147-127 BCE and the Almagest to the 2nd century CE, so the lead's c. 150 BCE-150 CE span is not one event. The geometric models are attributed to Hipparchus for the Sun and Moon and to Ptolemy for the planets; the sources opened do not date the models themselves.
cards.name: Geometric solar, lunar and planetary astronomy, Rhodes and Alexandria
cards.summary: Hipparchus on Rhodes and Ptolemy in Alexandria built geometric models of the Sun, Moon and planets with epicycles, which stayed the working astronomy for about fourteen centuries.
cards.description: Hipparchus made observations from Rhodes in the second century BCE, and his models of the Sun and Moon used eccentric and epicycle devices that he tested against Babylonian eclipse records. Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, set out geometric models of the Sun, Moon and planets in the Almagest, which was fundamental to astronomy from the second century CE to the late Renaissance. Britannica says the history of celestial mechanics until Kepler was mostly an elaboration of Hipparchus's model.
cards.origin_note: Britannica says Hipparchus adopted lunar periodicities known to Babylonian astronomers, a documented transmission; the epicycle and eccentric devices were already familiar to Greek astronomers, so the Greek geometric framework is not itself a transmission from Babylon.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the geometric framework served Islamic and European astronomy for many centuries, and Britannica says later celestial mechanics was an elaboration of Hipparchus's model.

events.label: 147-127 BCE
events.statement: Ptolemy cites more than twenty observations that Hipparchus made on Rhodes on specific dates from 147 to 127 BCE.
events.quote: more than 20 observations made there by Hipparchus on specific dates from 147 to 127

events.label: 2nd century CE
events.statement: Ptolemy's Almagest, which sets out geometric models of the Sun, Moon and planets, was conceived in the second century CE.
events.quote: From its conception in the second Century up to the late Renaissance, this work is fundamental in determining astronomy as a science.

sources.title: Ptolemy (Claudius Ptolemy) biography
sources.publisher: Florida State University, National High Magnetic Field Laboratory

open_questions: The date of Hipparchus's geometric models themselves is not in the sources opened; the earliest dated record of the framework is the Almagest, so a dated Hipparchan model is a question for later research.
Which of Rhodes or Alexandria is the better primary place: Hipparchus worked on Rhodes, Ptolemy in Alexandria, and the card gives both.
The Apollonius origin of the deferent-epicycle construction is named in search results but was not in the sources opened.
Coordinates are approximate and from general knowledge.

cards.lead: Venus and eclipse tables of the Maya
cards.note: The Dresden Codex is most likely a thirteenth-century painting, and its astronomical content draws on earlier almanacs, while the Xultun tables date to about 800 CE. The lead's c. 300-900 CE span is therefore not supported as a date for the tables, and the sources opened do not establish that the tradition was independent of Old World astronomy.
cards.name: Venus, eclipse and lunar tables of the Maya
cards.summary: Maya scribes recorded tables for Venus, eclipses and the Moon, with a wall set of such tables at Xultun about 800 CE and the Dresden Codex copies of later date.
cards.description: Astronomical tables painted on the walls of a structure at Xultun, Guatemala, were recorded in a building filled in around 800 CE, and their numbers relate to the synodic periods of Venus and Mars. The Dresden Codex contains a Venus table and an eclipse table, and the physical manuscript was most likely painted in the thirteenth century, although its almanacs reference Classic-period events from as early as the fifth century.
cards.origin_note: The sources opened describe Maya tables and their Classic-period dates but do not state whether the tradition was reached without contact with Old World astronomy, so independence is not established.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the tables served one culture's ceremonial calendar, with no later line shown in the sources opened.

events.label: c. 800 CE
events.statement: Two tables of astronomical reckonings were recorded on the walls of a structure at Xultún, Guatemala, which was filled in around 800 CE.
events.quote: As part of an urban renewal project circa 800 CE, Maya inhabiting what is now the Petén region of Guatemala filled residential dwellings with rubble and dirt before building over them.

sources.title: Ancient Maya astronomical tables (Physics Today, reporting Saturno et al., Science 2012)

open_questions: The Science 2012 paper by Saturno et al. was not opened; the Physics Today summary is used instead.

The Dresden Venus table's own early history is not established by the sources opened; the book cites the physical codex as thirteenth century (Bricker and Bricker 1992) or late fifteenth century (Bricker and Bricker 2011), and the two are not settled.
The Long Count and 260-day calendar are left for the timekeeping record, as the lead says.
Coordinates are approximate and from general knowledge.

cards.lead: Star calendars and the Pleiades year in Polynesia
cards.note: The Hawaiian Makaliʻi and Māori Matariki new-year associations are supported by a Bishop Museum-linked essay, but no source opened gives a date for when these calendars began, and the 'by c. 1000-1250 CE' date and the late eighteenth-century written record were not found. Te Ara's Matariki page was blocked by a verification page, so it was not read.

cards.lead: Seasonal star knowledge in Aboriginal Australia
cards.note: The Boorong star-and-season record is documented from Stanbridge's 1857 reading and 1858 printing, which is the first record the lead cites. Sources opened do not support the claim that stars timed the harvest of eggs, tubers and fish, nor that the knowledge was independent or of great antiquity, so origin is unknown and the card covers only the documented Boorong case.
cards.name: Boorong star-season knowledge, north-western Victoria
cards.summary: The Boorong of north-western Victoria kept a star-and-season calendar that Stanbridge recorded in 1857, a documented case of Aboriginal seasonal astronomy.
cards.description: The Boorong clan of the Wergaia language, living in the Mallee country near Lake Tyrrell, claimed to know more astronomy than any other people, and they tied constellations and stars to the seasons. William Stanbridge read a paper of their astronomy and mythology to the Philosophical Institute of Victoria in 1857, and it was printed in 1858. Hamacher and Frew used his list of Boorong objects and seasons to identify a nineteenth-century record of the outburst of Eta Carinae.
cards.origin_note: The sources record Boorong star-season knowledge as their own tradition but do not state that it was reached without contact with others, and no earlier date is established, so independence cannot be confirmed.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the calendar served one clan's seasonal round, and the sources show no later line of work resting on it.

open_questions: Whether any earlier date can be defended for Aboriginal seasonal star knowledge in this region; the sources opened give only the 1857 record.
The malleefowl and Lyra egg-timing association, and the harvest claims in the lead, need a primary source; the Malleefowl Victoria page was not used as it is not primary.
The Stanbridge 1858 paper itself was not opened; the quotation is taken from Hamacher and Frew's citation of it, which is in the saved text.

cards.note: The Stanford entry dates Leucippus only to the fifth century BCE, so c. 430 BCE, Abdera and Athens are not supported as stated. Whether atomism was first known anywhere is not settled by the sources opened, which leaves the first_known origin unsupported.
cards.name: Atomism of Leucippus and Democritus
cards.summary: The doctrine that matter is built of atoms moving in void, credited to Leucippus, who is known only to have lived in the fifth century BCE.
cards.description: Leucippus is credited with founding atomism, the view that everything is made of atoms and void, though his own contribution is unclear and his birthplace is given as Elea, Abdera or Miletus. Aristotle ascribes the foundation of the atomist system to him, and the doctrine is associated with Democritus. The sources opened describe the theory but do not establish its later reception.
cards.origin_note: The sources opened describe the doctrine within Greek philosophy and do not compare it with Indian atomism, so whether it was the first known achievement, or was independent of other traditions, is not settled.

impact.note: Kept from the lead; the later reception and the seventeenth-century revival, which the lead cites, were not checked in the sources opened.

events.label: 5th century BCE
events.statement: Leucippus, credited with founding atomism, is known only to have lived in the fifth century BCE.
events.quote: His dates are unknown, other than that he lived during the fifth century BCE.
